subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Lung cancer: histology, metastases, and complications
vignette: A 64-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents with a 3-month cough, intermittent hemoptysis, and wheezing. Chest x-ray shows a well-defined 'coin' lesion, and CT confirms a noncalcified 2.5-cm nodule. He has no fever or weight loss. Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in the United States.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this patient's most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A benign pulmonary hamartoma discovered incidentally on imaging
Primary lung cancer (bronchogenic carcinoma)
A solitary metastasis from an occult colon primary
Bronchial carcinoid tumor producing carcinoid syndrome
An aspergilloma within a preexisting pulmonary cavity

explanation_correct: Primary lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death. It typically presents with cough, hemoptysis, bronchial obstruction, and wheezing, and may appear as a pneumonic 'coin' lesion on chest x-ray or a noncalcified nodule on CT. This patient's heavy smoking history and symptoms are classic for bronchogenic carcinoma. Most cases are advanced at diagnosis, which is why early recognition of these findings matters.

explanation_incorrect.A: Hamartomas are benign, well-circumscribed masses found incidentally on imaging; they do not cause cough, hemoptysis, or wheezing and are not the leading cause of cancer death.
explanation_incorrect.C: Metastases to the lung are usually multiple lesions rather than a solitary coin lesion, and a metastasis would not itself be the leading cause of cancer death from a primary lung standpoint.
explanation_incorrect.D: Bronchial carcinoid tumors can cause wheezing from mass effect and carcinoid syndrome with flushing and diarrhea, but this patient lacks those features and has a classic smoking-related noncalcified nodule.
explanation_incorrect.E: An aspergilloma is a fungal ball within a preexisting cavity rather than a solid noncalcified nodule, and it is not the leading cause of cancer death or linked to smoking in this way.

educationalObjective: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death and presents with cough, hemoptysis, wheezing, and a coin lesion or noncalcified nodule.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Lung cancer: histology, metastases, and complications
vignette: A 58-year-old man is evaluated for a central lung mass. He has smoked two packs per day for 30 years, worked for 15 years in a uranium mine, and lives in a house with high radon levels. His father died of lung cancer. He does not use asbestos.
question: Which of the following statements best integrates his risk factors and the likely location and histology of his tumor?

options.text: Adenocarcinoma is most likely because it is centrally located and strongly associated with radon exposure
Small cell carcinoma is peripheral and is not related to tobacco smoking
Squamous cell and small cell carcinomas are central, tobacco-related tumors, and his radiation, radon, and family history further raise his risk
Bronchial carcinoid is most likely because it is always central and tobacco-related
Large cell carcinoma is central and has the best prognosis of all lung cancers

explanation_correct: Risk factors for lung cancer include tobacco smoking, secondhand smoke, radiation, environmental exposures such as radon and asbestos, pulmonary fibrosis, and family history. Squamous cell and small cell carcinomas are central tumors that are often caused by tobacco smoking. This patient's heavy smoking plus mining-related radiation, radon exposure, and a positive family history place him at very high risk for a central, tobacco-related tumor.

explanation_incorrect.A: Adenocarcinoma is typically peripheral and is the most common lung cancer in nonsmokers; it is not a central tumor caused by radon exposure.
explanation_incorrect.B: Small cell carcinoma is central and strongly tobacco-related, not peripheral and unrelated to smoking as this option claims.
explanation_incorrect.D: Bronchial carcinoid tumors may be central or peripheral and are not tobacco-related; they have an excellent prognosis and rarely metastasize.
explanation_incorrect.E: Large cell carcinoma is peripheral, highly anaplastic, strongly linked to tobacco, and has a poor prognosis rather than the best prognosis.

educationalObjective: Squamous and small cell carcinomas are central, tobacco-related lung cancers; risk also rises with radon, radiation, asbestos, pulmonary fibrosis, secondhand smoke, and family history.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Lung cancer: histology, metastases, and complications
vignette: A 70-year-old woman with advanced small cell lung cancer develops jaundice and hepatomegaly. Imaging also shows an adrenal mass and a lytic lesion in the femur with an associated pathologic fracture. Brain MRI reveals a contrast-enhancing lesion. No other primary malignancy has been identified.
question: Which of the following sets of sites best matches the classic pattern of extrapulmonary metastasis from primary lung cancer?

options.text: Liver, adrenals, bone, and brain
Spleen, pancreas, and kidney only
Skin, skeletal muscle, and thyroid as the predominant sites
Heart, spleen, and bone marrow as the first sites
Isolated ovarian and testicular metastases

explanation_correct: Lung cancer most often metastasizes to the liver (causing jaundice and hepatomegaly), adrenals, bone (pathologic fracture), and brain. The mnemonic is 'lung mets love affective boneheads and brainiacs.' This patient's findings map directly onto those four sites and are typical of advanced lung cancer.

explanation_incorrect.B: The spleen, pancreas, and kidney are not the classic metastatic destinations emphasized for lung cancer; liver and adrenal involvement is far more characteristic.
explanation_incorrect.C: Skin, skeletal muscle, and thyroid are not typical sites for lung cancer metastasis; the classic pattern involves liver, adrenals, bone, and brain.
explanation_incorrect.D: Although bone marrow can be involved, heart and spleen are not the characteristic early metastatic sites of lung cancer.
explanation_incorrect.E: Gonadal metastases are not the classic pattern; lung cancer preferentially spreads to liver, adrenals, bone, and brain.

educationalObjective: Lung cancer classically metastasizes to liver, adrenals, bone, and brain ('affective boneheads and brainiacs').

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Lung cancer: histology, metastases, and complications
vignette: A 66-year-old man who has never smoked presents with dyspnea. Chest CT shows multiple bilateral well-defined nodules rather than a single mass. Colonoscopy reveals a primary colon adenocarcinoma. No single dominant lung lesion is identified.
question: Which of the following best explains the multiplicity of his lung lesions?

options.text: Primary lung adenocarcinoma with multifocal growth driven by a KRAS mutation
A single bronchioloalveolar carcinoma presenting as hazy pneumonia-like infiltrates
Benign hamartomas, which are typically multiple and well circumscribed
Metastatic tumor deposits, because lung metastases are more common than primary lung neoplasms and usually appear as multiple lesions
Multiple bronchial carcinoid tumors, which commonly metastasize to both lungs

explanation_correct: In the lung, metastases (usually multiple lesions) are more common than primary lung neoplasms. The most common primaries that metastasize to the lung include breast, colon, prostate, and bladder cancer. This patient's known colon primary and multiple bilateral nodules fit metastatic spread rather than a primary lung tumor.

explanation_incorrect.A: Primary lung adenocarcinoma usually presents as a solitary peripheral mass; multifocal primary lung tumors are much less common than multiple metastases.
explanation_incorrect.B: Bronchioloalveolar carcinoma (adenocarcinoma in situ) classically appears as hazy infiltrates resembling pneumonia with a better prognosis, not as multiple discrete nodules secondary to a colon primary.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hamartomas are benign, well-circumscribed lesions found incidentally; they are not the usual cause of widespread bilateral nodules in a patient with a known colon cancer.
explanation_incorrect.E: Bronchial carcinoid tumors have an excellent prognosis with rare metastasis, so they would not produce widespread bilateral deposits.

educationalObjective: Multiple bilateral lung nodules are more often metastases than primary lung cancer, commonly from breast, colon, prostate, or bladder.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Lung cancer: histology, metastases, and complications
vignette: A 62-year-old heavy smoker has a large central hilar mass, superior mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and extensive hepatic metastases. Biopsy shows small, dark blue cells with scant cytoplasm and nuclear molding. Immunohistochemistry is positive for chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and neuron-specific enolase.
question: Which of the following best identifies this tumor?

options.text: Squamous cell carcinoma with keratin pearls and intercellular bridges
Adenocarcinoma with a glandular pattern and mucin positivity
Large cell carcinoma with pleomorphic giant cells and hCG production
Bronchial carcinoid tumor with nests of neuroendocrine cells and an excellent prognosis
Small cell carcinoma derived from neuroendocrine Kulchitsky cells, with myc amplification and chemosensitivity

explanation_correct: Small cell (oat cell) carcinoma is a central, undifferentiated, very aggressive tumor derived from neuroendocrine Kulchitsky cells, producing small dark blue cells. It is positive for chromogranin A, neuron-specific enolase, and synaptophysin, and commonly shows amplification of myc oncogenes. It is managed with chemotherapy plus or minus radiation. Bronchial carcinoid tumors are also neuroendocrine and chromogranin A positive but are usually central or peripheral nests with an excellent prognosis and rare metastasis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Squamous cell carcinoma is central but is defined by keratin pearls and intercellular bridges (desmosomes), not small dark blue neuroendocrine cells positive for chromogranin A.
explanation_incorrect.B: Adenocarcinoma is typically peripheral with a glandular, mucin-positive pattern; it is not a small-cell neuroendocrine tumor.
explanation_incorrect.C: Large cell carcinoma is a peripheral, highly anaplastic tumor with pleomorphic giant cells that may produce hCG; it lacks the neuroendocrine marker profile described here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Bronchial carcinoid is a neuroendocrine tumor that can be central or peripheral, shows nests of cells, has an excellent prognosis with rare metastasis, and may cause wheezing from mass effect or carcinoid syndrome with flushing and diarrhea; it does not match this widely metastatic oat-cell tumor.

educationalObjective: Small cell carcinoma is a central, aggressive neuroendocrine tumor of Kulchitsky cells that is chromogranin A/NSE/synaptophysin positive and often myc amplified.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Lung cancer: histology, metastases, and complications
vignette: A 58-year-old man with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer complains of proximal muscle weakness that improves after repeated muscle contraction. Laboratory studies show hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine. He also has facial swelling, weight gain, and purple striae. He reports no diarrhea or flushing.
question: Which of the following paraneoplastic processes best accounts for these findings?

options.text: PTHrP production causing hypercalcemia with secondary muscle weakness
Lambert-Eaton syndrome from presynaptic calcium channel antibodies, SIADH, and ectopic ACTH causing Cushing syndrome
hCG production causing gynecomastia and secondary hyperaldosteronism
Carcinoid syndrome from serotonin causing flushing, diarrhea, and weakness
Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy causing clubbing and joint pain

explanation_correct: Small cell lung cancer causes neurologic paraneoplastic syndromes including Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (strength improves with use), paraneoplastic myelitis, encephalitis, and subacute cerebellar degeneration, as well as endocrine syndromes such as Cushing syndrome from ectopic ACTH and SIADH causing hyponatremia. This combination of weakness, hyponatremia, and cushingoid features is classic for small cell carcinoma. The inappropriately concentrated urine in the setting of hyponatremia confirms SIADH.

explanation_incorrect.A: PTHrP causing hypercalcemia is characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma, not small cell carcinoma, and would produce high calcium rather than the hyponatremia seen here.
explanation_incorrect.C: hCG production with gynecomastia is associated with large cell carcinoma and does not explain Lambert-Eaton weakness, hyponatremia, or cushingoid features.
explanation_incorrect.D: Carcinoid syndrome with flushing and diarrhea is due to serotonin from bronchial carcinoid tumors, not small cell carcinoma, and would not cause SIADH or Cushing syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy with clubbing is associated with adenocarcinoma, not small cell carcinoma, and would not produce weakness, hyponatremia, or striae.

educationalObjective: Small cell lung cancer causes Lambert-Eaton syndrome, SIADH, and Cushing syndrome, as well as paraneoplastic myelitis, encephalitis, and cerebellar degeneration.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Lung cancer: histology, metastases, and complications
vignette: A 52-year-old woman who has never smoked presents with a peripheral lung nodule and progressive dyspnea. She has clubbing of the fingers and painful swelling of the wrists. CT shows a peripheral mass and, elsewhere, a hazy infiltrate resembling pneumonia. Biopsy shows glandular structures that stain positive for mucin, with tall columnar cells lining alveolar septa.
question: Which of the following best characterizes her tumor and its histologic subtype?

options.text: Squamous cell carcinoma with cavitation and keratin pearls in a central location
Adenocarcinoma, the most common primary lung cancer and the most common type in nonsmokers, with a bronchioloalveolar (adenocarcinoma in situ) subtype that grows along alveolar septa
Small cell carcinoma with neuroendocrine markers and SIADH
Large cell carcinoma with hCG production and gynecomastia
Metastatic breast adenocarcinoma producing multiple bilateral nodules

explanation_correct: Adenocarcinoma is the most common primary lung cancer, is the most common subtype in people who do not smoke, and is more common in females than males. It is typically peripheral, is associated with activating KRAS, EGFR, and ALK mutations, and causes hypertrophic osteoarthropathy (clubbing). The bronchioloalveolar subtype (adenocarcinoma in situ) shows hazy pneumonia-like infiltrates, grows along alveolar septa with tall columnar mucus-containing cells, has a glandular mucin-positive pattern, and carries a better prognosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Squamous cell carcinoma is central, strongly smoking-related, cavitates, and shows keratin pearls and intercellular bridges, not a peripheral mucin-positive glandular tumor in a nonsmoker.
explanation_incorrect.C: Small cell carcinoma is central, strongly smoking-related, and neuroendocrine with small dark blue cells rather than glandular mucin-positive structures lining alveolar septa.
explanation_incorrect.D: Large cell carcinoma is a peripheral undifferentiated tumor with pleomorphic giant cells and possible hCG production; it lacks glandular differentiation and mucin positivity.
explanation_incorrect.E: Metastatic breast cancer typically produces multiple bilateral nodules rather than a solitary peripheral primary with a bronchioloalveolar component and hypertrophic osteoarthropathy.

educationalObjective: Adenocarcinoma is the most common primary lung cancer, favors nonsmokers and women, is peripheral with KRAS/EGFR/ALK mutations and clubbing, and its bronchioloalveolar subtype has a better prognosis.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Lung cancer: histology, metastases, and complications
vignette: A 68-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history presents with cough and hypercalcemia. Chest CT shows a central hilar mass arising from a bronchus with areas of cavitation. Biopsy reveals malignant cells with abundant keratin and prominent intercellular bridges.
question: Which of the following best explains the hypercalcemia and the histologic findings in this patient?

options.text: Ectopic ADH secretion causing hyponatremia and small dark blue neuroendocrine cells
hCG production causing gynecomastia and pleomorphic giant cells
PTH-related peptide production by a peripheral adenocarcinoma with mucin-positive glands
PTHrP production by a central squamous cell carcinoma with keratin pearls and desmosomes
Serotonin secretion by a bronchial carcinoid with nests of neuroendocrine cells

explanation_correct: Squamous cell carcinoma is a central hilar mass arising from the bronchus, is strongly associated with cigarette smoking, and may cavitate. It produces PTHrP, causing hypercalcemia. Histologically it is defined by keratin pearls and intercellular bridges (desmosomes), matching this patient's tumor.

explanation_incorrect.A: Ectopic ADH (SIADH) causing hyponatremia and small dark blue neuroendocrine cells is characteristic of small cell carcinoma, not squamous cell carcinoma.
explanation_incorrect.B: hCG production with gynecomastia and pleomorphic giant cells is characteristic of large cell carcinoma; it does not cause hypercalcemia via PTHrP or produce keratin pearls.
explanation_incorrect.C: PTHrP can cause hypercalcemia, but adenocarcinoma is typically peripheral with glandular mucin-positive structures; the central cavitary mass with keratin pearls indicates squamous cell carcinoma.
explanation_incorrect.E: Serotonin-related carcinoid syndrome with nests of chromogranin-positive neuroendocrine cells is typical of bronchial carcinoid, not a cavitary central squamous tumor with hypercalcemia.

educationalObjective: Squamous cell carcinoma is a central, smoking-related hilar tumor that cavitates, produces PTHrP causing hypercalcemia, and shows keratin pearls and intercellular bridges.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Lung cancer: histology, metastases, and complications
vignette: A 61-year-old heavy smoker has a large peripheral lung mass with extensive nodal involvement. Biopsy shows highly anaplastic undifferentiated cells with marked pleomorphism and giant forms. He develops tender enlargement of the breasts. The tumor proves relatively unresponsive to chemotherapy.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this tumor?

options.text: Large cell carcinoma, a peripheral highly anaplastic tumor strongly linked to tobacco that may produce hCG causing gynecomastia and has a poor prognosis
Adenocarcinoma in situ, which has a better prognosis and hazy pneumonia-like infiltrates
Small cell carcinoma, which is chemosensitive and centrally located
Bronchial carcinoid, which has an excellent prognosis and rarely metastasizes
Squamous cell carcinoma with keratin pearls and PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia

explanation_correct: Large cell carcinoma is a peripheral, highly anaplastic undifferentiated tumor with a strong association with tobacco smoking. It may produce hCG, leading to gynecomastia, and is less responsive to chemotherapy, so it is often removed surgically and carries a poor prognosis. Histology shows pleomorphic giant cells, as seen here.

explanation_incorrect.B: Adenocarcinoma in situ (bronchioloalveolar subtype) presents with hazy pneumonia-like infiltrates and a better prognosis, not an anaplastic mass with gynecomastia.
explanation_incorrect.C: Small cell carcinoma is central, neuroendocrine, and chemosensitive (managed with chemotherapy plus or minus radiation), unlike this chemotherapy-resistant peripheral tumor.
explanation_incorrect.D: Bronchial carcinoid tumors have an excellent prognosis with rare metastasis and can cause wheezing or carcinoid syndrome, not an aggressive anaplastic tumor with gynecomastia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Squamous cell carcinoma is central and produces PTHrP causing hypercalcemia with keratin pearls, rather than a peripheral anaplastic tumor producing hCG.

educationalObjective: Large cell carcinoma is a peripheral, tobacco-related, highly anaplastic tumor that may secrete hCG (gynecomastia), is surgically treated, and has a poor prognosis.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Lung cancer: histology, metastases, and complications
vignette: A 66-year-old smoker has severe right shoulder pain and weakness with atrophy of the intrinsic muscles of the right hand. He also has right-sided ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis, and new hoarseness. Chest x-ray shows a mass at the right lung apex. He has no facial plethora or jugular venous distension.
question: Which of the following sets of structures are most directly invaded or compressed by this apical tumor?

options.text: Phrenic nerve and brachiocephalic artery only
Vagus nerve and esophagus, causing dysphagia as the dominant feature
Recurrent laryngeal nerve, stellate ganglion, and brachial plexus
Superior vena cava and right atrium exclusively
Intercostal nerves and spinal cord only

explanation_correct: A Pancoast (superior sulcus) tumor is a carcinoma, most commonly non-small cell lung cancer, at the apex of the lung. It produces Pancoast syndrome by invading local structures: the recurrent laryngeal nerve (hoarseness), the stellate ganglion (Horner syndrome with ipsilateral ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), and the brachial plexus (shoulder pain and sensorimotor deficits such as atrophy of intrinsic hand muscles). It can also compress the brachiocephalic vein (unilateral symptoms), phrenic nerve (hemidiaphragm paralysis with elevation on chest x-ray), and superior vena cava (SVC syndrome).

explanation_incorrect.A: The phrenic nerve can be involved, causing hemidiaphragm elevation, but the brachiocephalic artery is not a classic structure, and this option ignores the stellate ganglion and brachial plexus that explain his Horner syndrome and hand atrophy.
explanation_incorrect.B: Vagal or esophageal compression causing dysphagia is not the classic Pancoast syndrome; hoarseness here reflects recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement and the hand findings reflect brachial plexus invasion.
explanation_incorrect.D: SVC compression can occur with Pancoast tumors, but SVC syndrome alone would not explain the Horner syndrome and intrinsic hand muscle atrophy; the recurrent laryngeal nerve and brachial plexus are also involved.
explanation_incorrect.E: Intercostal nerve or spinal cord involvement is not the primary mechanism; the shoulder pain and hand atrophy arise from brachial plexus invasion and the eye findings from stellate ganglion involvement.

educationalObjective: An apical (Pancoast/superior sulcus) tumor invades the recurrent laryngeal nerve, stellate ganglion (Horner), brachial plexus, phrenic nerve, brachiocephalic vein, and SVC.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Lung cancer: histology, metastases, and complications
vignette: A 60-year-old woman with a malignant mediastinal mass from lung cancer develops facial fullness and swelling, distended neck veins, and edema of both upper extremities. She reports headaches and dizziness, and examination shows laryngeal edema. A chest tube and central catheter are in place, though no catheter thrombus is seen.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this condition?

options.text: Superior vena cava syndrome from impaired venous drainage of the head, neck, and upper extremities, a medical emergency that can raise intracranial pressure
Pancoast syndrome from an apical tumor invading the stellate ganglion
Horner syndrome from stellate ganglion destruction causing ptosis and miosis
Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion causing hyponatremia and cerebral edema
Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome causing respiratory muscle weakness

explanation_correct: SVC syndrome results from obstruction of the superior vena cava, for example by thrombus or tumor compression from a mediastinal mass or Pancoast tumor, or by thrombosis from indwelling catheters. It impairs drainage from the head (facial plethora), neck (jugular venous distension, laryngeal and pharyngeal edema), and upper extremities (edema). It is a medical emergency; severe obstruction can raise intracranial pressure, causing headaches and dizziness and increasing the risk of aneurysm rupture. Along with Pancoast tumor, Horner syndrome, endocrine paraneoplasia, recurrent laryngeal nerve compression, thoracic outlet syndromes, and pleural or pericardial effusions, it forms the SPHERE of local complications.

explanation_incorrect.B: Pancoast syndrome is due to an apical tumor invading the stellate ganglion, brachial plexus, and recurrent laryngeal nerve, producing Horner syndrome, shoulder pain, and hoarseness, not the diffuse venous congestion described here.
explanation_incorrect.C: Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) results from stellate ganglion disruption and does not cause facial plethora, jugular venous distension, or upper extremity edema.
explanation_incorrect.D: SIADH causes hyponatremia and can cause cerebral edema, but it does not produce facial plethora, jugular venous distension, and upper extremity edema from impaired venous return.
explanation_incorrect.E: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome causes proximal muscle weakness from presynaptic calcium channel antibodies, not the venous congestion and laryngeal edema of SVC obstruction.

educationalObjective: SVC syndrome is an oncologic emergency caused by SVC obstruction (tumor or catheter-related thrombosis), producing facial plethora, JVD, edema, and possible increased intracranial pressure.
